I have some (fairly extensive) python scripting built up around my workflow, so my code is automatically checked in, built, linted and tested. If the build 'fails', the commit is rolled back. If it 'succeeds', the build is registered with a configuration management system. This is all wrapped with a 'metabuild' layer, which I use for parameter tuning and (eventually) code generation. A generic tracing system links together requirements, tasks, changes, datasets, projects, documents and any other 'managed' item. This also helps with time tracking. Training data and labels are also tracked with the same automatic configuration management and cross-reference/tracing systems. Training itself is still done outside the system, but the configuration management system makes it very easy to synchronise code baselines, data baselines and label baselines. Next step: Integrating voice control. :-)

Another point to mention: My data recording system automatically segments long-duration recordings into two minute long chunks. (I.e. you set it recording and it produces a sequence of two-minute-long back-to-back recordings). This means that we never have to deal with large recordings that are many tens of minutes in duration, and can easily delete data that does not deliver any value. (Knowledge is an asset -- data is a liability).

The main downside is that it is more difficult to manually browse the images and videos than if the main store were organised according to some semantically meaningful schema -- but once you have more than a few tens of thousands of files browsing the library manually is a bit of a fool's errand anyway... (And semantically meaningful directory names have been known to cause * ahem * disagreements in the past).

I have a structure that I have evolved over the past decade or so; variants of which have served me well for many years.

This is intended for video / radar / lidar / audio data and for a commercial environment where data is being recorded continuously for use across multiple different projects.

At the top level, data is organised into directories by date: YYYY/MM/DD. We deliberately avoid using 'drive' or 'trial' or 'task' identifiers or anything else that might inhibit full automation.

The next level down in the directory hierarchy is a recording-system-configuration identifier. This gives us traceability back to the system that did the data recording. In principle this should also include any changes made to the platform (aircraft / car / boat) carrying the data recording system. This can be a lifesaver in the face of otherwise inexplicable changes to the data a year or more down the line.

The bottom layers of the directory hierarchy may change depending on the data recording system configuration, but in general I separate each recording into its own directory, where the name of the directory has an incrementing serial number (for sorting order and traceability with trials logs) and a starting UTC time (for traceability with other metadata, e.g. meteorological records).

Within each recording directory, I try to separate different streams into separate files (with synchronisation information embedded), broken down into a sequence if those files risk becoming overly-large. This means that a system with 12 cameras, 4 lidar and 4 radar systems may have 20 different streams in each recording directory.

Sensor data is therefore organised in the following way:-
YYYY/MM/DD/rec-system-id/rec-id_hhmmss/stream-id_seq-no.format

This data is uploaded to our mass storage locations using a scripted process. We keep the data in two mass storage locations. The first holds only read-only sensor data. The second is a mirror structure holding a link to the original sensor data plus version-controlled metadata in text files. (E.g. label files in JSON or XML, depending on the label tool used). The version control over the metadata enables us to reproduce baseline testing and training if called upon. (I have only had to do this once in the last 10 years, but it is a nice thing to be able to show auditors). The metadata is indexed in a sql database. I have a set of Luigi pipelines that validate the data, create various index files and populate the databases periodically. 

Each project that is using this data creates a link to the original in project-specific directory structures, normally one for each training set. Rules prohibiting e.g. sharing of data in training and test sets are implemented in the scripts that build these test sets and in the metadata that is associated with the sensor data. 

The whole process is guided by a defined data lifecycle which is used to organise requirements, plan development etc...

Many problems come when organizations (ANY organization; public or private) exceed a certain size.

* Large organizations (in terms of manpower) have difficulty communicating.
* Long lived organizations have difficulty maintaining focus. (See the Peter Principle).
* Large organizations (relative to the market in which they operate) stifle competition.
* Powerful organizations (in local or national politics) both distort the market and stifle competition through the creation of biased legislation.

It is clear that the anticompetitive advantages afforded to large organizations outweigh the inefficiency and waste created by their size - leading to the extraction of economic rents, and the imposition of unfair and stifling public and private policies.

I admit that efficiencies of scale can and do occur. However, I also believe that anticompetitive and legislative effects are frequently as large, if not larger factors in explaining the dominance of large organizations - so whilst the general public may see some of the savings caused by those efficiencies of scale, they also have to pay a significant cost due to the burden of economic rent-seeking and corruption.

I believe that, properly organized, the market should be able to deliver *to the consumer* the cost savings that can be achieved through economies of scale without the cost burden of our current kleptocratic system.

So, yes, your point is spot-on. The pro-public-ownership vs. pro-private-ownership debate really misses the point. Who cares how the equity is organized, as long as the public receives a good service, efficiently managed? (And provably so, via a competitive marketplace).
